items.title: ‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
paragraphs: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return to Brazil after winning a historic fourth term in power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro.

“This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.

A few hours earlier, Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from a first-round defeat in early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff.
“Today is a historic day,” Lula declared, before telling a sea of elated supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again. Democracy always, fascism never again.”
Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.

But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, prompting joyous scenes on the streets of São Paulo and cities all across Brazil. He won with 64.2m votes to Bolsonaro’s 59.8m, a 51.79% to 48.21% victory. It was at least 10m more votes than Lula secured in the first round.

Lula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, told the Guardian shortly after the result was confirmed: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed.

“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha said at the hotel where the president’s team was following the count in São Paulo.

Bolsonaro rejected the result, following in the footsteps of his father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

But political leaders and governments from across the spectrum were quick to recognise Lula’s victory. Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, tweeted: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, wrote: “The global progressive resurgence has just begun.”

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called Lula’s victory “a historic win for the global progressive movement” and said his government looked forward to continuing to collaborate on “shared values of democracy, social justice and climate action”.

Rightwing South American leaders also recognised Lula’s victory, with Chile’s president, José Antonio Kast, calling Lula to offer congratulations and Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, saluting “the Brazilian people for this democratic day”.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.”
A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said: “China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.”

There was silence from Donald Trump, whose administration had been rooting for a Bolsonaro victory that would have seen the so-called pro-Trump “orange wave” continue its sweep across the region into Latin America’s largest democracy.

In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the US had been accused of seeking to influence the result through a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure. Erika Hilton, a transgender lawmaker who recently became the most voted-for woman in Brazil’s congress, said those efforts had failed. “We have defeated the interference of the US government, which thought it could turn our country into its back yard. Brazil and the Brazilians are too gigantic to be anybody’s back yard,” she said.

Lula’s victory will also have profound consequences for the environment and the Amazon rainforest in what is the world’s most biodiverse nation. On the eve of the vote, the former environment minister Marina Silva had warned that Bolsonaro, if elected, would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rainforest destruction started by his father, whose 2019-22 administration coincided with a surge in deforestation.
On Sunday night, Silva was in a buoyant mood, telling the Guardian: “My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people.”

She said: “The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations.”

For Flávio Bolsonaro, the future looks bleak. As the scale of Lula’s victory became clear on Sunday night, the mood at the Brasília mansion where Bolsonaro was watching the count soured, with what had initially resembled a lively birthday party turning into something closer to a wake. Like football supporters heading for the exits midway through the second half because their team was being thrashed, crestfallen guests began heading home.
One of them approached the dozens of journalists waiting for Bolsonaro’s speech to shout that it was the “north-east’s fault”, insulting the region where Lula has historically won most of his votes.

One photograph circulated by Lula supporters showed a dejected Bolsonaro in tears, although it had been taken on the eve of the vote. Another image showed a red-faced Bolsonaro flanked by visibly mortified allies as they came to terms with their defeat. São Paulo’s pro-Bolsonaro governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, sat next to him covering his face with his hand.

On Paulista Avenue, where huge crowds had gathered to hear Lula speak, one reveller wore a costume of Flávio Bolsonaro behind bars. Some suspect the senator is likely to flee the country to the US once his term runs out in February and he loses parliamentary immunity. Bolsonaro is facing a series of federal police investigations over suspected misdeeds including money laundering, although he maintains he is innocent.
Lula supporters delighted in the idea that the far-right politician may soon join his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his coup attempt, in jail.

“Oh, how awful! Poor little thing!” João Maluf, a 27-year-old psychologist, shouted sarcastically as he held up his mobile phone to the crowd to show them a photograph of a visibly distraught Bolsonaro. “We want rid of these fucking Bolsonaros,” Maluf said.

items.title: Burnham leaves door open to referendum on EU free movement
paragraphs: The prime minister has left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the European Union.
Asked by broadcasters if he could introduce free movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no", but sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made.
He added that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options, with these expected to be set out around the time of the EU summit next month.
Asked about Burnham's comments, the prime minister's deputy spokesperson said he "isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any option" but "thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough".
"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the spokesperson added.
Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.
The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.
The prime minister is thought to be against the idea of leaping quickly to a return to freedom of movement.
Sources indicated no firm decision had been made on whether free movement would need to be rubber-stamped by a referendum.
Burnham is said to believe that a conversation about the UK's future relationship with Brussels needs to happen first.
Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.
Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.
The PM has stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

However, he has suggested potential options for the future could range from no changes to the UK-EU relationship, to rejoining the EU customs union, the single market or a new in-out referendum on full EU membership.
In an interview with the Sunday Times, external, Burnham said he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and the EU.
The PM argued that the type of migration had changed since Brexit, with more foreigners moving permanently.
In contrast, he suggested that when the UK was a member of the EU, migration was "generally younger people", who would spend a few years in the country before returning home.
However, Burnham added: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."
The Schengen Agreement, which the UK was not part of when it was in the EU, allows passport-free travel across member countries.
The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.
Burnham has argued that since Brexit, the UK has lost immigration control the country previously had.

"For instance, the small boats crisis has arisen in the last 10 years because we lost that returns agreement when people came here that we could work with other countries to return them," he told broadcasters.
The Conservatives and Reform UK both oppose a return to free movement with the EU.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch argued most people who voted for Brexit did so because they did not want free movement, while Reform leader Nigel Farage has said such a move would be "a total betrayal of Brexit Britain".
Farage said the prime minister was "all over the place" on the question of another referendum and should not agree anything at November's UK-EU summit without putting it to a general election.
However, the Liberal Democrats have argued that allowing freedom of movement would help economic growth.

items.title: T-Mobile’s new plans include swappable subscription perks
paragraphs: T-Mobile is launching new “T-Mix” plans that bundle wireless service with subscriptions to services like Netflix, Apple TV, YouTube Premium, Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, device promotions, and more, as reported earlier by Fierce Network. The Standard plan starts at $55 / month (with autopay) for one line and one “Pick,” which you can change up to four times during the year without changing the cost of your plan.

The Standard also offers up to 50GB of “premium” data, video streaming in 480p, unlimited 3G hotspot connectivity, and unlimited 2G in Canada and Mexico. Meanwhile, the mid-tier More plan starts at $75 / month for one line, two Picks per line, and unlimited data. It also adds up to 4K UHD video streaming, up to 60GB of high-speed hotspot data, and up to 15GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico.

The highest-tier Loaded plan, which starts at $95 / month for one line, bumps things up a little more, offering access to up to three Picks per line for the first three lines (T-Mobile caps this plan at 11 perks in total). The Loaded plan also comes with the same up to 4K UHD video streaming benefit, as well as up to 250GB of high-speed hotspot data and up to 30GB of high-speed data in Canada and Mexico.
The types of perks you can add vary depending on how many your plan supports:
As noted by CNET, you can also trade your Picks for discounts on a new phone.

T-Mobile says that you can change up your perks every 90 days, according to Fierce Network. However, T-Mobile notes that how often you can change your perks depends on the benefit that you choose. “Some benefits let you switch any time, others hold your Picks for a quarter or longer,” T-Mobile says, adding that some services will charge if you switch them outside the change window. T-Mobile also offers an annual selection period where you can reset all of your perks.

items.title: Drivers who killed mum and girl while racing jailed
paragraphs: Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed.
Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her daughter Lena Czepczor were killed when they were hit by an Audi TT RS as they walked to the girl's nursery on the A61 Scott Hall Road on 16 January 2023.
At Leeds Crown Court on Monday, Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was jailed for 12 years and Jasskamal Riyat, 37, for 16 years.
Sentencing the men, Judge Singh said the road was "not a race track" and told them the deaths had consequences that were "immeasurable", with an "immense" impact on those left behind.

Bhachu, of Grant Row in Adel, had earlier admitted two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, while Riyat, of Buckstone Avenue in Moortown, was convicted by a jury after denying he had been racing him.
The court heard the pair, who did not previously know each other, accelerated away from traffic lights on Scott Hall Road shortly before the crash.
Prosecutors said Riyat's BMW reached speeds of up to 89mph in the 40mph zone before Bhachu lost control of his Audi, mounted the pavement and struck Hulboj and her daughter.
Susannah Proctor, for Bhachu, told the court that her client was a "normal person who's made a massive mistake".
She said he "must live with himself in the knowledge of the devastation he has caused".
And she said: "He did not intend to cause this devastation but cause it he has."
Hulboj's fiancé Dominik Czepczor watched the sentencing hearing in court.
A statement from him was read, which said: "My whole world collapsed in one second.
"Every day I feel a huge void after their departure.
"We had so many hopes and dreams and in one moment it all ended.
"My dream was to have a wonderful family, and I must say that it came true for a short while, but that was taken away from me on January 16.
"Unfortunately, all that remains are wonderful memories and a constant fight for the next day, which is not easy."

Det Insp Paul Conroy, of West Yorkshire Police's Major Collision Enquiry Team, said: "A woman and her young daughter have died because of the actions of these men, and I know no sentence will ever feel enough to compensate for the lives that have been lost.
"This sentencing hearing though does mark the end of a long criminal justice process for Justyna and Lena's family.
"It is over two years since Bhachu admitted his part in this tragic incident and I know that the wait for justice has taken its toll.
"My thoughts are firmly with them today."

items.title: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn Brazil election around
paragraphs: The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.
Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".
"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.
On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.

The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.
In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".
Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.
Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.
Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."
By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.
Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.
"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."
In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.
"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.
She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."
Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.
In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.
"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

items.title: Microsoft’s new Surface Laptop Ultra update fixes reboot and display bugs
paragraphs: The firmware update should resolve screen flickering, slow reboots, and unexpected restart issues.
The firmware update should resolve screen flickering, slow reboots, and unexpected restart issues.
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra was blighted by some nuisance bugs at launch, but now the company has released some new firmware to resolve them. The October 22nd release addresses three notable issues in particular: screen flickering, unexpected restarts, and lengthy reboot times alongside unspecified “additional bug fixes and general performance improvements,” according to Microsoft’s announcement.

My colleague Tom Warren experienced some of these issues when he reviewed the Surface Laptop Ultra, finding that rebooting the device was “surprisingly slow” and that “moving a window around rapidly sometimes left a little trail.” He also ran into some speaker interference issues that were “loud enough to sound like firecrackers” and resolved them upon rebooting the Surface Laptop Ultra, but found that “it’s happened a couple of times now.” We’ve asked Microsoft if this is one of the additional bug fixes included in the update.
In its announcement, Microsoft says some additional steps “may be required” for Surface Laptop Ultra users after installing this firmware update:
We recommend that you restart your Surface to complete any remaining part of the installation. To restart your device, select Start, and then select Power > Restart.

The firmware update will be delivered to all Surface Laptop Ultra devices, but not every device will receive it at the same time. If you don’t want to wait around, you can manually install the update by following the instructions over on Microsoft’s driver and firmware page. The firmware update can’t be uninstalled or reverted to an earlier version.

items.title: 'Safety first' as wedding guests stranded on island after Storm Boelo
paragraphs: Guests attending a wedding on Lower Lough Erne in a County Fermanagh island ended up stranded after the ferry took on water during Storm Boelo.
At the weekend, the storm saw gusts of wind reach almost 80mph in some areas and led to flights and ferries being cancelled.

Guest Shéa Clarke, who was on Lusty Beg island said that, despite the weather spirits were high, the staff were "great and obviously it's too dangerous to cross and the boat can't cross so safety comes first".
"You could see the waves were rough and the wind was going," he said.
"Some people have slept in cars, some people have slept on sofas there's been eight people in one room sleeping on the floor.
"But the spirit has been good the craic is 90," adding as "long as we don't run out of Guinness or chips".
A boat has since been taking guests off the island.
A Met Office yellow warning for strong winds, mainly along the Antrim and Down coasts, lasts from 18:00 GMT on Monday until 03:00 Tuesday.
Olivia Millar, a cabin crew member based in London, was also a guest at the wedding and said the plan was to be in South Africa on Monday night.
"It hasn't felt like real life but everyone's been amazing and we've just made the most of it.
"We've drunk to pass the time and had a really good barbecue yesterday".
Staff at Lusty Beg Island Resort & Spa took care of guests who couldn't get off the island.
Michael Cadden, managing director at hotel, said they are "delighted at how staff and customers have dealt with this".
"The ferocity and the longevity of this storm was unlike anything we've experienced on the island before.
"This was a crisis, but we've now arranged to transport and are getting all our staff and customers safely home".
Kacper Dymarczyk, a bartender, was locked down with the guests and had to work through the storm.
"It was great craic, seeing other people drinking" he said as he laughed.
Dymarczyk added that there was "no concern" of running out of anything as they are "well stocked at all times".

Meanwhile in the Republic of Ireland, an ESB spokesperson said there are "a number of homes, farms and businesses still without electricity" on Monday morning, and that teams are working to restore the power to all properties.
About 5,000 homes, farms and businesses were still without electricity on Sunday evening in the Republic of Ireland.
In the Republic of Ireland, wind and rain warnings have also been issued for most counties along the south and west coasts on Monday evening.
Much improved weather conditions are expected on Wednesday with calmer and sunnier weather in the forecast.
Although some faults occurred overnight in Northern Ireland, and are showing on NIE's Powercheck tool, external, they are not believed to be storm related.
NIE said around 12,500 properties were without power at one stage after Storm Boelo.

items.title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’
paragraphs: Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.

A year after the fall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.
A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected to a travel ban and an asset freeze.
The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.

During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – the fastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.
The killings came at the end of an 18-month starvation siege by the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.

Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous, with testimony indicating routine detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.
Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.
A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UK warnings were sidelined in the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.

A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre from the Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudan said: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”
During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which has forced 14 million people to flee their homes – has developed increasingly into a drone war.
The latest strikes saw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.

items.title: Russell Brand asked assistant for female fan phone numbers, court hears
paragraphs: A former personal assistant of Russell Brand has told a court she was instructed to get phone numbers for the entertainer from female fans when she first started working with him.

Helen Berger, who worked closely with Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, said the request "felt uncomfortable" and, after seeking advice, she told the TV personality that she would not do that anymore.
Brand, 51, is accused of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault, and one charge of indecent assault.
The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.
Brand had an "insane sexual appetite", Berger told Southwark Crown Court in a written statement on Monday.
Berger left her job with Brand after she became "sick of him", she said. She added that he had sex with numerous women during the time she was his assistant.
She described a work environment where Brand would ask her if he could "go and have sex now" when frustrated with a particular task.
Berger added that she never "witnessed anything against the law" but that "everyone normalised and dismissed his behaviour" so it "made me think it was accepted."
She told the court that "peacock" Brand found random women online to satisfy his "insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night", but sex often made him depressed.
She told the court Brand used MySpace to find women for sex, and said: "At his house, women often came over and it was clear they were there for sex."

She recalled once finding a female celebrity asleep in Brand's bed while he was wandering around the house half-dressed, and said of the comedian: "He was like a peacock, women would always approach him."

Russell Brand's defence team says any sexual activity was consensual and accounts have been twisted in the light of a defamatory TV documentary in 2023 which made allegations of sexual abuse against the entertainer.
The prosecution is due to finish on Tuesday morning.

items.title: Part of Antarctica named after former BBC science correspondent
paragraphs: The naming of geographical features in Antarctica follows strict rules.

The Amos Channel was recommended by the UK Antarctic Place Names Committee, which looks after names for sites within the British Antarctic Territory, as well as South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.
Athena Dinar, from the British Antarctic Survey, said: "Jon's passion for Antarctica and engaging journalism offers something for every reader, viewer or listener.
"The naming of an Antarctic place in his honour is a fitting recognition of his outstanding contribution to the promotion of Antarctic research."

Amos joined the BBC in 1986 as a local radio reporter in Cambridge. He was part of the team that launched the BBC News website in 1997, and ran the online science desk for many years. He later worked as a BBC science correspondent across TV, radio and online, before leaving the organisation in 2024.

"Jon consistently highlighted the importance of Antarctic research, explaining not only what science is being done there, but why it matters for society, climate understanding and the global environment," said Fiona Fox, from the Science Media Centre.

items.title: Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance
paragraphs: The head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally with Donald Trump just days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.

Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.

Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.
She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.

Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference to VW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.

A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.

Döllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday that Audi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the US and create 4,500 jobs, even as VW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plants in Germany.

“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.
He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.

Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.

The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.
She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.
She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.

Volkswagen is locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.

Its German ​factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.
“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.

Trump is deeply unpopular in Germany and has riled its political mainstream by vocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party, according to polls, and has actively courted Trump’s support.

The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive in the Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.
Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports are helping the US economy.

items.title: Remarkable’s refurbished Paper Pro Move bundle is over $100 off
paragraphs: is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

The Remarkable Paper Pro Move is essentially a digital notepad, with a skinny 7.3-inch E Ink screen that’s easy to hold one-handed to jot down notes or ideas. At $449 new, it’s not exactly cheap, but buying refurbished is a way to save, as always. Remarkable itself offers the refurbished Paper Pro Move for that same price with a polymer Book Folio case and a Marker Plus that has a built-in eraser tool. It comes with a one-year warranty. If you’re alright with trading the one-year warranty for a 90-day one, Woot has the same bundle for about just $342.

That offer is available exclusively to new Woot customers, who can enter the code REMARKABLE at checkout to save 10 percent on their order through November 2nd. The deal is good for returning shoppers, too, costing $379.99.

The Paper Pro Move makes it easy to convert your handwritten notes to text, and to store files on third-party cloud services. You can also view your notes in Remarkable’s apps and screen share from your E Ink device. However, Remarkable’s Connect subscription (a free 50-day trial for new users/devices) and $3.99 per month thereafter offers access to a larger suite of features. With it, you can search your handwritten notes, import docs and articles to the device to mark notes on, get AI-powered summaries of your handwritten text (viewable in a browser), and more.

items.title: Unions suspend planned V&A strike after improved pay offer
paragraphs: A planned strike at the V&A over half-term has been suspended after an improved offer from its management.

Museum staff who were members of the Prospect and Public and Commercial Services (PCS) unions had voted to strike on Thursday and Friday in a dispute over pay and working conditions including inadequate toilet and hydration breaks. The strike would have closed the V&A’s main galleries in south Kensington, as well as V&A East, V&A Storehouse and Young V&A in east London.
The strike was suspended on Monday pending last-minute talks with the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, after the V&A management made an improved offer.

In a statement PCS said it had suspended strikes planned for 29 and 30 October “to allow Acas-facilitated talks to take place, following an improved offer from the museum”. Prospect and the V&A also confirmed the strike had been suspended while negotiations continued.

The unions are demanding a 4% pay increase for staff earning above the living wage, and for the V&A to become an accredited London living-wage employer within 12 months. They also want time-and-a-half pay for bank holiday working.

On conditions, they are seeking improvements to working during heatwaves and better food at the museum’s east London sites. In July, when staff first voted to strike, a V&A spokesperson said “extensive measures” had been introduced to help staff during the heatwave. These included additional rest breaks and closing some galleries during the hottest periods.
The dispute has previously involved two separate two-day strikes in September.

A V&A spokesperson said: “All V&A museums will be open this week, including all exhibitions, free displays and planned half-term activities. While we are working to reinstate as much of our public programme as possible, unfortunately some events may still be cancelled or postponed – visitors are encouraged to check our website before travelling.

“We welcome this opportunity for constructive discussions with our trade union colleagues. Our latest pay offer delivers an average 4.18% pay rise and a 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues; increased bank holiday pay to 1.5, alongside a sector-leading bonus scheme and a subsidised food offer for staff at all V&A sites.”
Paula Lamont, Prospect’s national secretary, said: “We will be entering talks in good faith and hope that a resolution to the dispute can be found.”
Earlier this month, Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, called on the V&A’s director, Tristram Hunt, a former Labour MP, to get involved in the negotiations.

He said: “Prospect members are dedicated to their jobs, and it is these dedicated staff who make the museum the world-class attraction it is. That Tristram Hunt can’t even be bothered to take part in the negotiations himself shows the level of disdain in which he holds his staff.”

The London living wage is now £15.45 an hour. While the V&A has said all its staff are paid at least this rate, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors are not. V&A Dundee, which is not involved in the dispute, is an accredited living-wage employer.

items.title: AI giant Anthropic files for an IPO that could break records
paragraphs: Anthropic is taking a big step toward a blockbuster stock listing that would rank among the biggest IPOs ever. Patrick Sison/AP Photo hide caption

The artificial intelligence startup Anthropic, maker of the hugely popular Claude AI models, has taken a major step toward holding an initial public offering that analysts expect to be one of the biggest ever.
Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion.

That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June. Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range.

The filing of a public version of a registration statement called a Form S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission is a major milestone in Anthropic's meteoric rise. It was launched just five years ago by a breakaway group of OpenAI researchers, led by Dario Amodei, who were concerned that that company, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Anthropic has since become a juggernaut, and OpenAI's biggest competitor, with some of the most widely used AI models on the market. But the company has faced controversy, including a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used and questions about Amodei's dire warnings on AI risks.

Still, the prospectus highlighted Anthropic's bullishness about the technology. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.

In its prospectus, Anthropic highlighted breakneck growth — in revenue, income and losses. The company said its revenue in the first half of the year rose 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, vs. a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
Anthropic has yet to turn an annual profit, and said it booked a loss of nearly $81 billion in the January to June period, up from $13 billion during the same six months last year.

In a statement emailed to NPR, Raj Joshi, senior vice president in the corporate finance group of Moody's, the ratings agency, called Anthropic's swing in adjusted operating income from negative to positive territory "a strong positive for the AI ecosystem."
U.S. stock indexes were up on Monday after Anthropic's early-morning announcement.

The filing comes at a volatile time in the stock market for AI-related companies, as investors waver between exuberance about the positive effects AI could have on the economy and concern about safety and the tsunami of investment in the technology.

The IPO, which could happen as soon as November, will be one of the most eagerly anticipated public share offerings in years. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, is also planning an IPO, but those plans are temporarily on ice, with Altman ruling out a listing this year as "ill-advised" in the face of swirling AI safety concerns.

"Going public has a lot of advantages. It brings in capital for growth. It makes it easier for you to raise additional capital elsewhere. And it makes it possible for your existing investors to cash out," said Jim Angel, an associate professor and markets specialist at Georgetown University.

But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.

With SpaceX already trading publicly, Anthropic's IPO could test investor appetite for AI businesses at a time when markets are jittery about whether they can be profitable enough to justify the mind-boggling sums of money being invested in AI. SpaceX's shares soared briefly after the listing, but have come back down to around $150, where they started trading.
In May, at its last private fundraising round, Anthropic had a post-money valuation of $965 billion.

The balancing act for companies trying to ride the AI wave is real. The data center and infrastructure provider CoreWeave saw its share price plummet this month when investors got nervous about its ability to finance its expansion plans and its bond yields leaped. Other major players, including Intel, Meta and Nvidia, have also been buffeted by concerns and watched their share prices slide in recent weeks.

Debt financing has been a growing concern as AI-related companies scramble to raise money to meet demand at a time when interest rates are poised to keep rising as the Federal Reserve tries to douse stubborn inflation.

The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation.

Amodei himself has issued some of the AI world's sharpest warnings about the possibility of AI spiraling out of control and causing harm, and urged AI companies to "pace the frontier," or to slow the development of their most capable models.

Anthropic has also clashed with the Pentagon this year over how the military can use its models. Amodei has drawn a line in the sand when it comes to using Anthropic's AI for autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans.

In response, the Pentagon blacklisted Anthropic and designated it a "supply chain risk" — a label previously reserved for entities affiliated with U.S. adversaries. Anthropic has sued the Pentagon in two federal district courts. Those legal battles remain ongoing.
Editor's note: This story was updated to add additional information from Anthropic's prospectus. Oct. 26, 2026

items.title: Chris Brown given suspended eight-month prison sentence over nightclub attack
paragraphs: US singer Chris Brown has avoided jail after striking a man twice in the head with a glass tequila bottle in a London nightclub.
The R&B star was given an eight-month prison sentence, suspended for 12 months, over the attack at private members' club Tape in Mayfair, in the early hours of 19 February 2023.

Brown's vocal coach, rapper Omololu Akinlolu, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months' imprisonment, suspended for 12 months. Both men, who had pleaded guilty to affray, were also ordered to pay £1,500 costs.
Judge Tony Baumgartner said Brown's use of the glass bottle to hit the victim twice over the head "was plainly dangerous", adding that the violence of the attack was "intense".
The sentence means Brown will not be imprisoned unless he commits another offence during the 12-month period of suspension.
The court heard Brown's attack on music producer Abraham 'Abe' Diaw left the victim in need of hospital treatment for his injuries.

In sentencing, Judge Baumgartner said: "The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous, it carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained."
CCTV footage was shown where Brown struck Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head, and then hitting his shoulder.
Sentencing Brown, Judge Baumgartner said: "This was not planned violence. It was nevertheless serious violence by two people in a crowded nightclub."
The judge told Brown: "Violence of this kind in a crowded nightclub is serious, it creates an obvious risk, not only to the person against whom it is directed, but also to others nearby."
He added that Brown's conduct was "particularly dangerous" and that he had to be "physically pulled away" from the attack.
The judge said Brown's fame, commercial success and professional standing "do not entitle you to special treatment - the law applies equally to everyone".

But judge Baumgartner also said he had noted Brown's guilty plea, compliance with bail conditions, and the impact a custodial sentence would have on Brown's children, and said the singer's "risk of further offending is low".
Brown and Akinlolu pleaded guilty to a charge of affray at Southwark Crown Court in July.
The singer had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied, and which were subsequently dropped.
These were assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon.

Following Brown and Akinlolu's guilty pleas, the CPS released a statement outlining that Brown had approached Diaw on the dance floor, hitting him over the head with a glass bottle twice, before Akinlolu then punched Diaw in the head.
"They continued their assault whilst the victim attempted to flee through the club," the CPS said. "The victim was kicked while he was seated defenceless on the floor."

Judge Baumgartner told the pair that while he had concluded they had both crossed the threshold to be jailed, this year's changes to sentencing laws meant that he had to put off doing so, unless there were exceptional reasons.

"I have considered whether the seriousness of the offending, taken together with the need for punishment and deterrence, amounts to exceptional circumstances requiring immediate imprisonment. I have concluded, in relation to each of you, that it does not," he said.
"These were serious offences deserving of custodial sentences, but the circumstances do not justify displacing the [new legal] requirement that those sentences be suspended."
On Monday, the court was shown three pieces of CCTV footage from inside Tape nightclub on the night of the attack.
The attack lasted no more than 20 seconds, but Brown could be seen hitting the victim four times with a tequila bottle, twice to the head.
Prosecutor, Heidi Stonecliffe KC, described the weapon as a "heavy square-shaped tequila bottle" and said Diaw was approached by Brown at around 03:00.
The footage showed that the nightclub was very small and packed at the time.
The defence described Chris Brown as a "dedicated and a loving father of four children," someone who is "positive and present".
The singer is described as having lived "a good and law-abiding life" since his last conviction in 2013.
The events in Tape nightclub were described by the defence as a "short and deeply regretted incident".
Brown's defence lawyer told the court that he apologises to all those present at the club at the time of the attack.
"This is an ugly and unattractive incident," Sallie Bennett-Jenkins KC said.
"It is, however, an incident which was very short-lived, lasting something more than 17 seconds but no more than 20.
"It is something which undoubtedly would have caused distress to those who are present and for which Mr Brown... offers a profound apology to all those present."
The court heard Akinlolu "genuinely believed" that Brown was "under attack" when he joined the attack, punching Diaw.
Brown was described as being like a "brother" to Akinlolu, his lawyer Laurie-Anne Power KC told the court.
She added: "He genuinely believed him to be under attack and became involved, and thereafter accepts his initial involvement very quickly evolved into the events he has pleaded guilty to."
Diaw was taken to St Mary's Hospital in London after the attack. Ms Stonecliffe KC said he was discharged with "pain relief and a diagnosis of head injury and superficial injury of the knee".
An MRI scan taken in early March showed a "high grade injury to a ligament on the inner side of the left knee", the court heard.
Defending Brown, Ms Bennett-Jenkins KC said there was a "relatively low level of force" and disputed how significant the injuries were.
The defence argued that the attack left no fractures or broken skin and there was an absence of serious injuries.
Diaw, the victim, was "not supportive of the prosecution" and "withdrew" his support some time after the incident, the court heard.
Brown and Akinlolu stood up and faced one another and clasped hands after the judge concluded his sentencing remarks before walking out of the glass dock.
There were loud cheers outside the court as Chris Brown left the building as he appeared to stop to sign an autograph.
After the sentencing, Brown shared a video from inside his car on his Instagram story, showing him looking out the window before turning to the camera and giving a thumbs-up.

Affray is an offence under the Public Order Act and a person is deemed guilty in law if they use or threaten "unlawful violence towards another" with their behaviour, leading someone to fear for their personal safety.
Brown, 37, is considered one of the biggest stars in R&B, with a string of hit songs including Turn Up The Music, Ayo, Freaky Friday, Run It, Forever, Yeah 3x and Don't Wake Me Up.

items.title: US Marine indicted for murder and robbery of woman in Japan
paragraphs: A US Marine has been indicted on suspicion of murdering and robbing a woman in Japan earlier this month in a case that has triggered protests, Japanese media reports.
Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who was stationed at US Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, was arrested on suspicion of killing Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa.
Prosecutors have now indicted him for allegedly strangling Yagi with a telephone cord and then stealing her backpack and wallet on 3 October, media reports, citing the indictment document.
It wasreported Ballard had denied the allegations, but Asahi Shimbun and Kyodo News cited investigators saying he has made some statements suggesting involvement.
Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings.
Yagi's death has caused outrage in Japan, with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi describing the crime as "brutal and heinous".

Earlier this month, the Marine Corps said it was "actively cooperating with Japanese authorities, in response to allegations of serious criminal actions by a Marine" and extended condolences to the victim's family.
It is the latest case involving a US serviceman in Okinawa, which hosts the highest concentration of around 55,000 US soldiers stationed in Japan.

Previous criminal cases have sparked anger and protests, the largest of which took place in 1995, when tens of thousands took to the streets following the abduction, beating and rape of a 12-year-old girl.

In 2024 alone, there were four sexual assault cases involving US troops in Okinawa, including that of air force member Brennon Washington, who was given five years for the rape and kidnapping of an underage girl.
In 2025, US marine Lance Cpl Jamel Clayton was sentenced to seven years in prison for sexually assaulting a woman.
Okinawa Governor Genta Koja said the prefecture has repeatedly demanded that the US take action to prevent such incidents, and said he sees the alleged crime as a sign of a lack of discipline.

The prime minister said her government has registered a "strong" protest with the US and called for "strict disciplinary action against US military personnel and thorough measures to prevent a recurrence of such incidents".

People in Japan have been voicing anger, with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo earlier this month. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice, with one user saying: "Enough is enough."

items.title: Protests, tourists and the Kremlin: Georgia at a crossroads – photo essay
paragraphs: In the heart of Tbilisi’s Armenian quarter, Avlabari Square is where crowds gather for the “Saturday March”. Every weekend, protesters head towards the Bridge of Love, reach Freedom Square and march towards parliament, chanting slogans against Irakli Kobakhidze’s government.

Demonstrators in Tblisi take part in the Saturday March, when pro-European parties and movements march through the historic centre to protest against the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which critics accuse of being pro-Russian.

For years, the target has been the same: Georgian Dream, the ultraconservative party in power since 2012, accused of growing authoritarianism and, through its decision to suspend EU accession talks, moving the country closer to Moscow again. Georgia was granted EU candidate status in 2023.

Monday marks two years since the contested parliamentary elections on 26 October 2024 that ignited the political crisis. Protests began two days later and peaked on 28 November, when the government announced it would not put the opening of EU negotiations on its agenda before the end of 2028.
A woman walks along one of the bridges connecting three Soviet-era towers on Nutsubidze Street in Tblisi.

Two homeless people shelter in the decaying entrance to the Metallurgist sanatorium, an abandoned Soviet-era hotel. Formerly a famous spa town, Tskaltubo hosted 120,000 visitors a year, including Joseph Stalin, who came to enjoy its 22 sanatoriums. After the collapse of the USSR, the area fell into decline and most of the sanatoriums and hotels were abandoned. Today, only a few hundred tourists visit the town’s sole remaining spa centre.
Books lie scattered across rooms at the Museum of Local Traditions in Tskaltubo, Georgia, where the library is being rebuilt.

Georgia is experiencing a curious paradox: while many of its citizen would like the country to be more democratic and form closer ties to Europe, Georgia is attracting growing numbers of tourists drawn to its historic sites, post-Soviet atmosphere and unspoilt landscapes.

While the streets of Tbilisi have become the stage for one of the longest protest movements in recent history, in 2025 the country, according to data from the Georgian National Tourism Administration, recorded a high of more than 5.5 million international tourist visits: an 8.4% increase on 2024 and almost 10 times the number (about 560,000) who visited the country 2o years ago.

A tourist walks through one of the rooms of the Joseph Stalin Museum. The Soviet dictator was born in Gori in 1878, and the museum was established in 1937 near his birthplace. Transformed into a museum glorifying Stalin in 1957, it remained open even after the collapse of the USSR and the 2008 war with Russia.
Travellers come not only from Europe; many are from the Middle East, and large numbers come from Russia.

After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, tens of thousands of Russian citizens relocated to Georgia, bringing money and opening businesses, but also exerting strong pressure on the property market by buying homes across the country.

This has fuelled discontent among a population that, mindful of the early 1990s wars against Russian-backed separatists in South Ossetia and Abkhazia, and the brief August 2008 war fought against Moscow, also in South Ossetia, continues to consider Russia an occupying power.

An abandoned Soviet-era building in Chiatura – one of Georgia’s most important mining towns, where manganese is extracted. The industry faces a severe environmental and economic crisis, which has prompted continuing protests by workers.
An inhabited Soviet-era building in Chiatura.

The mythical land of the Golden Fleece and the Argonauts – the ancient Greeks called the journey to reach it “the longest possible voyage” – is now a republic roughly the size of Ireland, with a population of fewer than 4 million. Georgia emerged from the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Sandwiched between Russia and Turkey (alongside Armenia and Azerbaijan), it offers a wealth of attractions that draw tourists: quaint mountain villages scattered along the Georgian Military Road, ancient Orthodox churches overlooking rivers and valleys, fascinating post-Soviet cities with a decaying atmosphere, wine with a millennia-old history, a lively “Las Vegas” on the Black Sea (the port of Batumi) and a dynamic, cosmopolitan capital.

Visitors relax on the pebble beach north of the historic centre in Batumi, with a large container ship heading into the port in the background. Home to numerous casinos and a rapidly growing tourist destination, Batumi is known as the ‘Las Vegas of the Black Sea’ and is also an important commercial port.

Tbilisi, with its rich underground scene and repurposed industrial spaces, is reminiscent of 1990s Berlin. One of its crown jewels, a true symbol of national independence, is the Rustaveli theatre, renovated 20 years ago by the billionaire who founded Georgian Dream in 2012: Bidzina Ivanishvili. Now in his 70s, Ivanishvili served as Georgian prime minister between 2012 and 2013 and made his fortune in Russia during the 1990s after the Soviet collapse.

People on a train in Tbilisi. Opened in 1966 to facilitate travel in a city that stretches along the river and is built on steep slopes, the metro network was the fourth-largest in the Soviet Union. Today, the metro, which has two lines and 23 stations, carries 400,000 passengers a day.
A woman takes a selfie overlooking Tbilisi from Mtatsminda Park.
Tourists take photos near the Leghvtakhevi waterfall in Tbilisi, while others capture the scenery from the funicular leading to Mtatsminda Park.

Georgians attend a concert at Mtatsminda Park. Founded in the 1930s, the park stands 770 metres above sea level and features restaurants, a rollercoaster, a concert venue, and a large ferris wheel visible from much of Tbilisi.

Today, the relationship between Georgia and Russia is built on a contradiction that is difficult to resolve. After the 2008 conflict and the consolidation of Russian military control over Abkhazia and South Ossetia (regions accounting for approximately 20% of Georgian territory), diplomatic relations between the countries were severed.

Yet economically, Moscow remains a partner that is difficult to replace: trade, tourism, remittances and Russian capital, along with energy imports, prop up Tbilisi’s economy, which, despite strong growth – GDP rose by 7.5% in 2025, marking five consecutive years of expansion – continues to be affected by unemployment, low wages, widespread poverty and, in many rural areas, depopulation.
But Georgia’s predicament extends beyond its domestic political crisis, reflecting wider geopolitical tensions.
A woman picks flowers in the hills surrounding Gergeti Trinity church, beneath Mount Kazbek.
Worshippers leave Gergeti Trinity church after mass on 16 July. The day marks the Gergetoba festival, also known as the Day of Spiritual Love.

Relations with Brussels have deteriorated recently; the EU has criticised the Georgian government’s record on the rule of law and political repression. And many believe a strengthening of Moscow in the Ukraine war could significantly increase its ability to exert pressure on the Caucasus.
Both of which make the question inevitable: does the future of a vulnerable Georgia – internationally isolated and with limited domestic support – also hinge on the fate of Ukraine?

items.title: The Simpsons' brilliant parody of The Nightmare Before Christmas is proof that handmade creativity is on the rise
paragraphs: Over the last couple of years, I've worried that AI will take over animation, and that everything will end up looking slick and perfect… but really boring. This weekend, though, has eased my fears.

On Friday, Laika’s Wildwood, the studio’s sixth feature, opened in cinemas worldwide. I've already written about how its focus on stop-motion is what we all need in the AI era. So it's fantastic news that the movie seems to be doing well at the box office so far.

Shortly after that, we got The Simpsons’ Treehouse of Horror XXXVII opener: a stop-motion homage to The Nightmare Before Christmas. Bart is Jack Skellington, Marge is Sally, Homer is the two-faced Mayor, Santa’s Little Helper is Zero, and Ned Flanders is a bug-stuffed Oogie Boogie. Together, they belt out a parody version of This Is Halloween, replaced by the words "Simpsons Halloween".
The Simpsons | Nightmare Before Christmas Treehouse of Horror XXXVII by Stoopid Buddy Stoodios - YouTube

Since 1990, the Halloween specials have sat deliciously outside the show’s continuity. Characters die gruesome deaths, Springfield gets destroyed, but the following week everything's back to normal. In the new opener, Lisa (dressed as a witch) even spells it out in song: "Halloween episodes are not canon". And brilliantly, that freedom extends to the animation style itself.

Thematically, this sequence and Laika's Wildwood have almost nothing in common. But what matters is that both were made the slow, handmade way: with puppets, physical sets, and people moving them frame by frame. That's truly a lovely thing to see.

The Simpsons sequence came from Burbank’s Stoopid Buddy Stoodios, best known for Robot Chicken, which uses retro toys, action figures and dolls in stop-motion animation to deliver pop-culture parodies.

The studio could have used 3D printing. It chose not to. Co-founder John Harvatine IV told Animation World Network. “We kind of just did old school the whole way, from sculpting by hand." Similarly, sculptor Jim McKenzie told Entertainment Weekly: “I think in a time of AI, to be involved with something that’s truly handmade, it’s very special these days." Hear, hear.

It’s fitting that The Simpsons chose Nightmare as its Halloween tribute. When director Henry Selick’s chaotic classic arrived in 1993, it proved that a stop-motion feature could be a mainstream hit, and set him on the path to Coraline, the film that launched Laika.
The Simpsons - Nightmare Before Christmas - At Stoopid Buddy Stoodios - Behind The Scenes - YouTube

Back then, stop-motion was seen as very old hat, a thing of the past. Three decades later, it feels like a refreshing antidote to AI and overly slick CG, and this Simpsons opener plays right into that idea.
These gruesome puppet caricatures might only be on screen for half a minute, but they’re part of a much bigger fightback for handmade animation and creativity in general. Two enthusiastic thumbs up.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

items.title: Endangered turtles and ‘exceptional’ coral at risk from Woodside’s gas drilling in WA, watchdog says
paragraphs: Woodside Energy’s plan to drill for gas off Western Australia’s north-west coast could significantly damage “exceptional” coral reefs and it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level, according to advice from the state’s independent environmental watchdog.

A draft letter from WA’s Environmental Protection Authority written in 2023, seen by the Guardian, sharply criticised Woodside’s proposal to develop the Browse gasfield, saying its plans to protect endangered turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.

Woodside, Australia’s largest fossil fuel company, is hoping to win approval next year to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast. Scientists have warned it could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem, which is home to more than 1,500 species, many unique to the area.

EPA staff presented the draft letter to the authority’s board for approval in December 2023. In February 2024, two months after it was discussed, the EPA sent a letter to Woodside saying its preliminary view was to reject development of the vast gas reserve.

It was a significant setback to Woodside’s plan to drill more than 50 wells and pipe the gas 1,000km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant adjacent to the world heritage-listed Murujuga rock art.

The company won approval last year to run the North West Shelf until 2070. But it needs the gas from the Browse basin – Australia’s largest undeveloped source of gas – to feed it. If the processing plant was to operate until 2070 it could lead to about 88m tonnes of carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere each year after the gas was burned.

The concerns presented in the letter to the EPA board show the pressure on authorities to recommend against the gasfield development being approved. The development is being assessed by both the state and commonwealth EPAs. Ultimate decision-making power lies with environment ministers.

The letter shows the EPA board was advised by its staff that there was a threat of serious or irreversible harm to turtles and whales and more generally due to oil spills. The threats were considered serious enough that the staff said the precautionary principle should be invoked. It meant the EPA should assume the worst possible outcomes could occur.

In response to this near rejection of its proposal, Woodside added explosive-driven shear rams to its drilling plans, a step that could allow it to seal a leaking well in seconds. The company said this would reduce the “longest credible duration” of a “highly unlikely” well blowout, and potential oil spill, to about 12 hours.

Not all companies have faith in shear ram technology. In 2024, fellow WA gas exporter Chevron rejected “pyrotechnic shearing” technology for its own wells, describing it as unproven and impossible to test in the field.
A Woodside spokesperson said if the shear rams failed it would deploy a capping stack to stop the oil flow within 16 days.
But the EPA was advised in 2023 that if a well leaked for 13 days it was possible there could be “irreversible consequences” to Scott Reef.

The draft letter said Sandy Islet, a part of Scott Reef considered critical to the survival of endangered green turtles, would be threatened if the seabed subsided after Woodside extracted gas from beneath it. It said a proposal to top up the sand on the islet, where about 1,000 turtles breed each year, was a “high-risk” measure and its success was “likely to be limited”.

Woodside said it would address this by changing its plans so that no wells would be drilled within 20km of Sandy Islet. It also said the flaring of gas, which produces bright light that can confuse turtle’s navigation, would be restricted.

The EPA board was also told noise, traffic and vessel strikes would have a significant impact on pygmy blue whales migrating between Timor and southern Australia. Scott Reef is the only known whale feeding ground on the migration route, according to the draft letter.

Woodside’s spokesperson said the company understood whales did feed at Scott Reef, but that this was opportunistic and the area was not as important as the ocean off Perth and other areas further south. Woodside agreed that Scott Reef and Sandy Islet had exceptional environmental value and it was important to protect them for future generations.

Glenn Walker, Greenpeace head of nature, said Woodside’s plans to address the concerns raised by the EPA did not go far enough and relied on “fanciful and unproven technology” to prevent a catastrophic oil spill.

“It would be a major backflip for both the WA EPA and the national EPA to now recommend approving this project,” he said. “It is now critical that these regulators maintain their independence from corporate and political influence and reject this destructive project.”
Greenpeace last week nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing based on its ecological and scientific values.
Just two of the current nine-strong WA EPA board were in place when the watchdog told Woodside it was set to reject Browse.

One of those – the current chair, Darren Walsh – said in a statement the assessment had been lengthy because it was a complex project in a sensitive area. He said a final state report and recommendations on the proposal would be provided to the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, when it was complete. There would then be a three-week public appeal period before a decision was made.

A spokesperson for the national EPA said the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.

Issues that have to be considered under national law include the potential impact on pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the marine environment in commonwealth waters and Murujuga rock art near the gas processing facility.

items.title: The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs
paragraphs: The explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence in France and across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say.

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday to protest underfunded schools, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures.
Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis, as households grapple with high and rising prices.
The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude, but the grievances are common.

Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France, but soaring energy costs were having a major impact.
Fuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.
More fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state.

France’s high public debt, stagnant economy, and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position.
France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund.
Australia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%.
Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity.
“If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said.

Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver.

“One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places, but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said.
The evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows.

In contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom.
“All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, who said France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”.
“The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.”
President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending.
“There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said.
The bond market reflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory.

France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position.
That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011.

Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long.

“We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.”

While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes.
“At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.”

items.title: To buy or to rent? – level 1
paragraphs: Twin sisters Morgan and Lisa move into the same kind of house. Morgan buys her home. Lisa rents hers.

Morgan must pay a lot of money in the beginning. She repairs the house when things break. After 30 years, Morgan pays off her home loan, and her house becomes worth a lot of money. She buys the house for 400,000 dollars. After 30 years, she can sell it for 1.3 million. Lisa pays rent every month. She does not pay for repairs. She saves money. She has a retirement account. After 30 years, she pays 900,000 dollars for rent. But she has 500,000 in her retirement account.
In the end, Morgan makes more money by buying. But Lisa is free to move. She can spend on hobbies, not a house.

Difficult words: twin sister (a girl who is born at the same time to the same mother as another child), rent (the money which you pay when you live in someone’s house or flat), retirement account (an account where you save money for the time after finishing work).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: To buy or to rent? – level 2
paragraphs: To see if buying or renting a home is better, we can follow twin sisters Morgan and Lisa over 30 years.

Morgan bought a house for 400,000 dollars and she used a mortgage loan. She had to pay a large down payment and all repair costs herself. She spent 1.4 million in total, but her house became worth 1.3 million. On the other hand, Lisa rented her house, which means she started with much smaller costs. Her landlord paid for all home repairs, and Lisa invested her saved cash into a retirement account. After 30 years, Lisa spent 900,000 dollars on rent, but her investments grew to 500,000.
While buying gave Morgan a stronger financial outcome in the long run, renting provided Lisa with more freedom, flexibility to move, and lower monthly costs early on.

Difficult words: mortgage loan (a bank loan for buying a house), down payment (the money which you pay at the beginning when you buy a house), landlord (a person or company which owns a house or flat and rents it).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
