items.title: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
paragraphs: Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.

But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.
Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.

We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.

But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy.

In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue.
Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks.

Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.

This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.

To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.
For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.

When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.
Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.

Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman, a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters. Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough.

So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.

The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek, a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.
Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."

Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.

Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.

Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.

This story includes reporting from Ruth Tam, Sylvie Douglis, Frank Festa, Andee Tagle, Manoush Zomorodi and Margaret Cirino. This story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is Beck Harlan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter. Follow us on Instagram: @nprlifekit.

items.title: See how Big Tech is transforming Spain's landscape
paragraphs: ZARAGOZA, Spain — Aragon's rugged plains stretch out under a clear blue sky, the buildings visible as "a few tiny cubes sprawled like a throw of dice" across the terrain — as George Orwell wrote in Homage to Catalonia, of his time here during the Spanish Civil War in the 1930s. Today, excavators eat the earth, carving huge chunks of the landscape in the race to build the behemoths of the AI boom.

This drought-stricken region of northeast Spain has become the focus of American companies searching for locations to place their energy- and water-intensive data centers. In Aragon, Amazon Web Services promises to spend almost $40 billion to build multiple vast complexes — one alone as large as 600 American football fields. Microsoft and the asset management firm Blackstone are among those following suit, signing agreements to build data centers that will transform this region and the livelihoods of its inhabitants.

Heavy equipment excavates an area adjacent to an Amazon data center currently under construction in Cuarte, Spain, on Sept. 29. Local authorities have approved dozens of data center projects for U.S. Big Tech and other companies that will transform the character of this region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Even as other countries enact regulations to curb the expansion of data centers (and Spain's national government weighs new restrictions), Aragon's regional government is welcoming the companies with open arms. Touting themselves as the "Virginia of southern Europe" after the U.S. state with the largest concentration of data centers, they are taking the bet that hosting data centers will bring jobs and prepare the region for the economic shifts they believe AI will bring.

"This is a new economy that is evolving, and it's very difficult to foresee how many activities are going to be coming around it," said Eva Valle, the economic counsellor for the regional government. "But they are coming."

An Amazon data center, currently under construction, is seen in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. Aragon authorities say they are betting that hosting data centers will place them at the center of a "new economy" they believe AI will bring. But many local residents and activist groups believe these projects are delivering an environmental crisis. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

An Amazon data center, currently under construction beside the quiet village of Cuarte, Spain, on Sept. 29.It's being built beside the village on land close to a protected wetland. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Companies building data centers in Spain's Aragon region say they will mostly rely on renewable energy. But the centers will also sometimes be powered by on-site generators. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

The companies were drawn to the region with promises of large tax breaks and fast-tracked planning permissions that give these data centers a special status usually reserved for the general interest of the local population. This order gives them the power to expropriate land, strips local mayors of veto powers, and restricts the time the public has to object to 23 working days. (For the recent Amazon Web Services development, the regional government opened the window to oppose the project over the Christmas period. Opponents of the project believe they did this to try to push it through at a time when people would be paying less attention, though the government denies this.)

The Sotonera reservoir, which serves population centers and farms in the provinces of Huesca and Zaragoza, is seen in Tormos, Spain, on Sept. 29. This is one of Spain's driest regions that, with climate change, is already suffering from repeated drought. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
The rapid approval process for these large and hyperscale facilities has left many in Aragon feeling excluded from decisions that will profoundly impact their region and lives.

Farmland that is to be developed into a data center complex is seen in Botorrita, Spain, on Sept. 28. Residents of Botorrita village say they first learned of the project when they found the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. The government of Aragon is fast-tracking planning permissions under a procedure that also significantly cuts the time the public has to object. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

The first time Silvia Baselga and her family learned of the data center soon to tower over their home was when they noticed the survey markers poking out of the ground on the other side of their garden wall. "When we saw this, we went to the city hall and said, 'OK, we want information. This is really close to our house.'" But the local council told them they had no information. Only when the planning documents were later made public did they learn that the outer perimeter of the data center is to be built within 300 feet of their home in the hilltop village of Botorrita. The plans showed that the complex will be larger than the village itself.

Residents point to an area that is to be developed into a data center complex in Botorrita, Spain, on Sept. 28. Residents say the planned complex comes to within 80 meters of the garden wall of a family living at the village edge. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Baselga's parents retired here for the tranquility of a life spent in a tight-knit village community. Their home looks out over fields and gently rolling hills. To try to block the noise the data center will emit, Baselga believes the company will build a 20-foot-high wall, as happened in a nearby village. "We're going to open the window and see nothing," she said. Friends regularly visit at night to gaze at the stars in this rural setting. Baselga said the center's 24-hour security lights will block out the night sky. "It's going to be like living beside a prison."

Centers like these are set to be built across Aragon — 27 in total, according to official documents — some by Spanish and other firms, but most by American companies, taking up about 7 square miles of land. At least one is built partly on ground originally classified as protected for natural ecosystems. The companies promise employment. Amazon Web Services told NPR it will create 6,200 permanent jobs once these centers are built. But many residents fear they will also deliver an environmental crisis.

Julio Enfedaque stands at the edge of a construction site where an outflow pipe will be installed that he says will carry water from a nearby Amazon data center in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. Farmers in the region are concerned about the water these data complexes require. In this region already affected by frequent droughts, they fear they will be in competition for the resources to grow their crops. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

The data centers will consume many times the current electricity needs of the region and require large amounts of water to cool their servers in one of Spain's driest regions, one that's been repeatedly blighted by drought.

Julio Enfedaque drives across the parched land his family has farmed for generations. This year it barely rained for four months, and the government cut the amount of water available for irrigation by two-thirds. "Even if they say the data centers won't take the water that we need for agriculture, I am sure it's going to become very complicated to farm like my ancestors used to." Enfedaque has advised his nephews to find different careers and leave the land.

Julio Enfedaque carries some alfalfa in Villanueva de Gallego, Spain, on Sept. 27. He fears the construction of so many water-hungry data centers in this region will leave him without enough of the resource to grow his crops. His family has farmed here for generations. He believes this way of life is so under threat that he says he is advising his nephews to find other careers. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Amazon Web Services says its data centers will draw water only after temperatures hit 86 degrees Fahrenheit and that they are investing millions of dollars to help fix leaking water pipes and working with farmers to use AI technology to make their water use more efficient. "We're trying to not only use as less [sic] water as possible, but also to help those communities where we operate have the best infrastructure," David Blázquez, Amazon's head of public policy for Spain and Portugal, told NPR.

But the company remains opaque about how much water each center will use. Blázquez said it's "a company policy not to publish water usage per site." Regional figures show Amazon's three existing data centers, which are much smaller than what is planned, used 68 million liters — 48% more than the company had originally told regional officials they would need.

Swallows fly in front of wind turbines near Huesca, Spain, on Sept. 29. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Perhaps an even bigger problem is the energy these centers need to run. Unlike many data centers in the U.S., which are powered by natural gas, companies in Aragon say they will rely mainly on renewable sources (though they also have diesel generators on site). Blázquez says Amazon Web Services has secured "a hundred renewable projects in Spain," including 17 in Aragon.
While that energy is carbon-free, ecologists and biologists warn that additional wind projects could have their own devastating consequences for the environment.
The region is full of hunting grounds for vultures and other birds of prey and an important stop for migrating birds.

Ornithologist José Antonio Pinzolas looks at a dead vulture, killed by a wind turbine, in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, solar panel farms and wind turbines, which has alarmed many local residents with the high energy use, noise pollution, danger to wildlife and heat generation they are known for. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
Ornithologist José Antonio Pinzolas looks for raptors and vultures, flying near dozens of windmills, in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption
"The vultures look for the thermal air currents to lift them. But they run straight into the windmills — for them it's like flying through knives," explained José Antonio Pinzolas, an ornithologist.

Aragon's own environmental agency has warned that wind farms in this area pose a high risk of collision to the endangered red kite and other protected raptors, and has documented an increase in bird and bat deaths in recent years as the renewable sector expands.
"I've collected ospreys, golden eagles, kestrels by the dozen, black vultures," said Juan Ballesteros, a nature protection officer for the local government.

Juan Ballesteros, an agent with the Protección de la Naturleza (Environmental Protection), removes a dead vulture, killed by a wind turbine in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Juan Ballesteros, an agent with the Protección de la Naturleza (Environmental Protection), removes a dead vulture killed by a wind turbine in Rueda de Jalón, Spain, on Sept. 27. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Ballesteros used to love his job for its access to wildlife. Now, he said, he spends his days placing the corpses of birds killed by turbine blades into body bags. Ballesteros met NPR as he arrived to collect the body of a young Eurasian black vulture that lay dead on the ground, its wings splayed in the dirt at the foot of a wind turbine.

Blázquez told NPR, of the damage to this important habitat that the expansion of wind and solar farms causes, that Amazon Web Services "definitely shares those concerns." He said they work with renewable energy companies that comply with environmental legislation. But Pinzolas said the growing number of bird deaths shows the current protections in place are not working.
Environmental groups say the overall impact of wind turbines on birds isn't being properly assessed.

Several groups have crowdfunded together to mount a legal action to try to stop Amazon Web Services' expansion in Aragon. The court case challenges the Aragon government's fast-tracked approvals of the plans. "We have concerns about water consumption, about energy consumption, the impact on some other industries and on the environment," said Luis García,, an activist with Ecologistas En Accion, one of the organizations involved in the case. He said the economic benefits of data centers are not great enough to justify the "huge damage they do to the environment."

Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

One recent weekend in the region's capital, Zaragoza, an avenue filled with demonstrators protesting against a new data center to be built at the edge of a forest by the city. Residents fear the heat and noise of the complex will destroy a tranquil space that is a haven during the hot summer months.

Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

"This is a worthy fight as all the worlds invades us, to save this pine forests, to save the environment, against this voracious capitalism that thinks only of economic interests and not of people," said Marian Rams, a local resident with white hair dyed in hues of pink, green and blue. "They want to swap nature for data centers."

Hundreds of protesters walk through the streets of Zaragoza, Spain, on Sept. 27. The Spanish region of Aragon is seeing a huge surge in data center construction, which has alarmed many local residents due to their high energy use, noise pollution and heat generation. Microsoft and Amazon are among those building in the region. Michael Robinson Chávez/for NPR hide caption

Nearby, a little girl no older than 5 chanted along with the demonstrators. Her mother, Ana Domezian, walked alongside her with her second child, a baby, nestled in a carrier against her chest. "If we don't fight now for what we have," she asked, "what are we going to leave to them in the future?"

items.title: Oracle's debt is growing. The tech giant's investors are concerned
paragraphs: Oracle, the multinational tech giant has taken on a lot of loans to build up its AI capacity. But Oracle's investors are not happy with this piling debt load.

items.title: Proms, parties and gender politics: amazing photos from American dancefloors – and what they tell us about a changing nation
paragraphs: Life magazine launched in 1936. Its aim: to show the US the world, in pictures. At a time when television was still an experimental medium, a golden age of photojournalism brought the outside world into people’s homes. Life ran weekly until 1972, spanning a transformative time in US culture. Photographers were dispatched across the globe, covering wars, political manoeuvres, social trends, hemlines and Hollywood. And in December 1936, the magazine dedicated its cover feature to dance, with dancers from the new School of American Ballet gracing the front page. As such a vividly visual medium, dance would become a regular feature in Life’s pages across the years.

When I was asked to write the text for a new book featuring a collection of dance-themed images from the Life archive, it was a kid-in-a-candy-shop situation. For a dance fan there were some absolute gems to be found: the great George Balanchine crafting his ballet The Seven Deadly Sins – and cooking dinner in his Manhattan apartment; Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev taking New York in a piece headlined The Hottest Little Team in Show Biz; or an ageing Agnes de Mille going full-throttle in rehearsal.

But the archive told a much bigger story than that. It was fascinating to see the reflection of society through the way people danced: in ballrooms, nightclubs, proms and parties. In the array of social dancers: from the waltz and tango to the lindy hop, mambo, twist and the frug, themes of the 20th century play out. You can see a story of growing individualism in the shift from structured couple dancing to going freeform on the dancefloor – gender politics, too, as it was out with “May I have this dance?” and in with the democracy of the disco. Life columnist Albert Goldman asked: “Has there ever been a decade for dance like the 60s?” as he wrote of a power shift from the stage to the dancefloor, from the professional performer to the “inventive amateur”. There’s the birth of the teenager, too, bringing an explosion of pop culture and spreading dance trends on TV shows such as American Bandstand.

The archive also tells a story of the US’s shifting relationship with race, showing dancers in segregated bars and newly desegregated schools. But more than that, we see the way music and dance styles from Black communities and from Latin America were adopted, appropriated and absorbed into the US mainstream, whether tap, jazz, Charleston or cha-cha-cha.

Dance even had something to say about cold war politics and paranoia. For a series comparing American and Soviet education systems, which found the US lagging worryingly behind, Life took photos of Moscow students in a dance class to demonstrate their iron-clad discipline, compared with easygoing American schools. The magazine captured visiting folk dancers from the USSR, as well as reporting on Khrushchev denouncing the dancing in a Hollywood film, and by extension, casting judgment on western culture.

So much of life can be observed through dance, in the ways people choose to move their bodies and how they display themselves, how they relate to each other, celebrate and communicate. There’s a real treasure trove of images to explore.
LIFE. Let’s Dance is published by Taschen.

On the set of Can-Can, 1959 (main image) The sheer raucous joy in this picture of Shirley MacLaine and Juliet Prowse leaps off the page, captured on the set of movie musical Can-Can, the story of a Belle Époque Paris cabaret whose dancers are arrested for public indecency. It was a stance approved of by Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev, who was visiting the 20th Century Fox studios during filming and pronounced the dance routines depraved.

Willa Mae Ricker and Leon James, 1943 Ricker and James were members of Whitey’s Lindy Hoppers, one of the finest, and most awesomely acrobatic, dance troupes of the 1940s. The lindy hop originated among Black dancers in the clubs of Harlem (it was named after pilot Charles Lindbergh’s “hop” over the Atlantic in 1927) but by 1943, Life was calling the lindy hop “America’s national dance”.

The Rockettes, 1958 Modelled on high-kicking British group the Tiller Girls, all-American precision dance troupe the Rockettes took things up a notch with their machine-tooled synchrony. Launched in 1925, they’re still going strong today, proving the enduring allure of the showgirl (Taylor Swift can’t be wrong), and have even trademarked their signature dance technique.

Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev in La Bayedère 1965 It is hard to imagine now that two ballet dancers could be as famous as Margot Fonteyn and Rudolf Nureyev were in the 1960s. Rudimania peaked on the Royal Ballet’s 1965 tour to the US, when mounted police were stationed outside New York’s Metropolitan Opera House to save Nureyev from being mobbed.

School prom, 1967 Teens dancing at the annual prom at Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Ten years earlier, after the supreme court had ruled against segregation in public education, Arkansas’ governor called up the National Guard to stop nine Black students enrolling at the same school. Life’s journalist at the prom reported that “the school sees itself as desegregated rather than integrated”.

Michael Caine on the dancefloor, 1966 Such a keen dancer he was once known as Disco Mike, here’s Michael Caine at an LA club. Decades later he gave a tutorial on doing the twist on Jonathan Ross’s chatshow, a dance craze that had swept the world, meriting a seven-page feature in Life in 1961. From hipsters to socialites to suburban grandmas, everyone was caught up in “pulsating, gyrating, hip-swinging mania”, it reported.

items.title: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
paragraphs: The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites.
Governments and some of the world's biggest companies, including Amazon, are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws.
The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them.
Amazon was targeted in multiple attempts, which it said occurred before an embargo on the warning was lifted. It added that it was unclear how actors knew about the vulnerabilities.
A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), as well as its counterparts in the EU and Australia, earlier urged those who use PHP to apply the fixes.
"Where immediate remediation is not feasible, organisations should consider taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated," the NCSC said in a statement., external
PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.
When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web.
Surrey Centre for Cyber Security Prof Alan Woodward said the flaw affects some 30 million websites.
As well as the scale of the flaw, Woodward said the nature of it means "an attacker can get their own code on to the webserver and run it and basically do whatever they like."

"They can steal data , they can go to other parts of your network. All sort of things like that - even plant a backdoor to get in later on, so it's pretty serious," Woodward told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.
Cyber security researcher Ryan Austin, who has been researching PHP security for the last 20 years, said he discovered the flaw in the programming language.
He told the Today programme it was "the most serious vulnerability I've ever found" which "started with a hunch that I would not have been able to scratch without AI".
Austin described PHP as "one of the first web languages that powered the early internet".

"It's in a lot of places that you wouldn't expect to be that are basically very core to how the internet runs in a lot of ways. It's like all the old things that are in a house that you know keeps it [running] but you don't really think about," the PHP researcher said.
Listen to BBC Radio 4 Today programme's interview with Ryan Austin at 0810 BST on BBC Sounds
Amazon announced on Wednesday that it had identified a "PHP2Shell exploitation attempt" that occurred on 17 October.
In the attack, an anonymous internet address attempted to target weaknesses in one of Amazon's decoy or "honeypot" systems, the company's security chief CJ Moses said.
The use of an anonymous IP address suggests that the activity was conducted by a "threat actor", he said.

While the PHP Foundation intended to release its discovery later this month along with a complete fix for the problem, usually referred to by software developers as a "patch", details of the flaw were leaked on social media on Tuesday.
In subsequent attacks on Amazon that occurred on 21 October, "the actual payloads and choices in anonymisation infrastructure varied, suggesting these were multiple actors," Moses said.
The attacks occurred after the leak, but before the embargo was lifted on the PHP warning.
The use of AI means that "more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed", Moses added.

The PHP incident has "demonstrated how quickly AI is changing our cybersecurity landscape", Australian Council on AI Strategy CEO Anna-Maria Arabia told the BBC, as "what used to take months, to expose a vulnerability, is now taking days".
She warned that threats would only become more commonplace as AI technology rapidly improves. It is "not going backwards, in other words", she said.
The PHP flaws went undetected for at least a decade.
Cyber-security firm Wiz has estimated that "roughly 70%" of the internet is affected, though the BBC is unable to independently verify that figure.
The websites for several BBC programmes including Doctor Who and The Traitors are currently inaccessible.
They have not confirmed a link to PHP - BBC News has approached them for comment.
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) said it had followed guidance to take its website offline, "in view of the critical security issues affecting PHP".
Edinburgh and Oxford council websites also went offline on Wednesday, but are now accessible.
The Dutch cybersecurity agency went offline as a precaution, and Finland's government shut down its public web services. Wikipedia also took down parts of its website.
This was in line with advice issued by governments, including the US, to take websites down if the flaws could not immediately be fixed.
The US National Security Agency said that the vulnerabilities identified "often provide a direct path to the server's file system or database".

It could allow attackers to "steal sensitive data, disrupt services, or move deeper into a network. These vulnerabilities are flaws in PHP itself, not in the hosted application or its configuration," the NSA said in a later update.
OpenAI called the discovery, "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".

items.title: Dame Judi Dench: 'I can't do a play, a film or read anymore'
paragraphs: Dench also discussed meeting American actor Sidney Poitier, who became the first black man to win the Academy Award for best actor in 1964.

She was appearing in Amy's View in New York when Poitier came backstage after a performance. She recalled that director Richard Eyre was in her dressing room, giving her notes, when there was a knock at the door.
Dench said she felt as if she were in a wind tunnel when Poitier walked in, adding: "It was thrilling."
Asked what she had said to him, Dench replied: "Not much, a bit of an open mouth. So charming. Very tall."

The conversation then turned to Dench's love of Shakespeare. She recalled watching her brother play King Duncan in Macbeth when she was nine and said the moment sparked her passion for the playwright.
"He walked on and he said 'What bloody man is that?' I thought, 'oh my God, this is for me'. He said 'bloody', did you hear that?"
She also admitted to being " besotted" by Shakespeare's sonnets: "I just love them."
"It's the rhythm of it. It's the rhythm of your heart," she added, "it's the way he's summed up so simply the way that any of us feel about, well, anything."

items.title: What is PHP and why did it spark an international cyber-security alert?
paragraphs: For more than a decade, serious flaws had gone undetected in the technology underpinning much of the internet.
It took artificial intelligence (AI) to bring them to light and caused a global cyber-security alert.
The vulnerabilities lie within a programming language called PHP, which has been used internationally since the 2000s to build websites.

Governments and cyber-security agencies around the world are scrambling to contain the fallout of the discovery on Wednesday, and have urged website operators to install a new emergency fix or consider taking their platforms offline.
Cyber-security firm Wiz - one of the companies whose researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities - described the flaws as the "most severe" ever detected by AI.
OpenAI, whose technology was used to find the flaws, called the discovery "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory".
Most people may not have heard of PHP - short for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor - but they most certainly interact with it daily.
PHP powers a vast number of platforms, including online shops, Wikipedia and WordPress – the content management system behind many websites like blogs.

When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web, Paul Spain, chief executive of Gorilla Cyber Security, told the BBC.
But due to a flaw that could allow attackers to take control of affected web servers without authentication and steal sensitive data, everything built on PHP was left exposed.
AI could make such attacks easier and faster, Spain said, estimating that the flaw could affect "millions and millions" of websites.
It would be "disastrous" if hackers or countries weaponised the flaw and seized private data from websites, said cyber-security researcher Jill Slay from the University of Adelaide.
The alert has disrupted services globally, from gaming platforms to government portals and online forums.
That includes Wikimedia - the organisation behind the online encyclopaedia Wikipedia - which took down a number of its systems as a precautionary measure.
Sites and pages have been taken offline by the Finnish government, Edinburgh council and the BBC, with the Netherlands' cyber-security agency also pulling its website.
Websites like the University of Geneva's were taken offline on Wednesday
A number of Scotland's public organisations, including councils and health boards, have also taken their websites offline.
Some experts warn the vulnerability could leave poorly maintained websites, particularly those belonging to smaller organisations with limited security resources, at greater risk.
More attempts to exploit these flaws are likely in the coming weeks since the technical details are now being made public, cyber-security researcher Salil Kanhere from UNSW Sydney said.
Developers of the PHP platform on Wednesday rolled out patches to fix the vulnerabilities that had been lurking in their software for years.
"All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately," the company said.
Authorities and security organisations around the world have echoed those warnings to website operators to secure their platforms.

The US National Security Agency told all organisations that use PHP to take their systems offline if they were unable to patch them immediately, adding that the flaw could provide a "direct path" to exploit a system's database.
"These risks are serious enough to require immediate patching across United States Government departments and agencies," the agency said.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice and told organisations to check for "backdoors installed by an attacker".
Its counterparts in the EU, Singapore and Australia have also issued similar alerts.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP.
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged people to check if their publicly available websites ran on PHP
"We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight," Takaichi wrote on X.
"If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk," she said.
Tech companies are also racing to secure their systems.
E-commerce giant Amazon said it was targeted in multiple attempts days before the public disclosure of the PHP issue. It is unknown how the potential attackers knew about the vulnerability.
The vulnerabilities were found by researchers at the security firms Calif and Wiz.
The researchers used advanced AI tools that are able to analyse code and find flaws much faster than humans or older systems can.
"Modern software is incredibly complex, and some vulnerabilities can remain undetected for years," Kanhere said.
"The underlying bugs weren't new; what changed was our ability to find them," Kanhere said.
Details of the discovery leaked online this week, forcing the PHP platform's developers to rush out its announcement of the security flaw and its huge scale.
The incident "highlights how AI can uncover security flaws" but also how it can "help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits," OpenAI said in a blog post.
The ChatGPT-maker said it had released a program to check if the PHP platform is secure.

"Many of these flaws stem from the way software were built in the past, which were built for functionality and not with security in mind," said Ryan Ko, at the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre.
Website owners are being urged to secure their websites with the latest version of PHP.
The PHP software patch is a small, routine fix for most tech teams, Spain said.
The US National Security Agency has urged "heightened awareness" in the coming weeks and to closely monitor updates from software vendors.
"Vigilance in applying patches related to those systems is paramount," it said.
The onus lies mainly on website operators, but users should stay alert for any security advice issued by affected services, such as requests to change passwords, Kanhere said.
He warned people to be alert to any phishing messages exploiting the publicity around the incident too.

items.title: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened
paragraphs: AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction.

Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco.

Amid increasing anti-datacentre activism in the US and Europe, they are calling on ministers to create a “compact” that would show how communities can benefit from hosting datacentres, including allowing councils that host them to retain more tax revenues.

The move by the Sovereign AI Leadership (SAIL) taskforce reflects rising concern among tech companies that arguments that have blocked datacentre developments in parts of the US are taking hold in Britain. Microsoft has promised to invest $30bn (£22bn) in UK AI infrastructure.

Microsoft has built a datacentre in Acton, London and another is under construction in Newport, but wants to build several more facilities and is engaging with local and national leaders, including the prime minister, Andy Burnham, over the balance between the potential benefit of AI to the economy and public opposition to datacentres.

The SAIL group said: “In the United States, organised local opposition has stopped fully permitted datacentre projects, and moratoriums have been announced even in states that are otherwise pro-growth.

“Reporting from those places shows that AI itself is only a surface-level concern; distrust of corporate and government promises, fear of stranded assets and electricity costs run deeper. The same arguments have begun to appear here.”
It added: “Britain has a window – we think of roughly 12 months – to build a compact that earns public consent before that pattern takes hold.”

The taskforce is calling for the government to create a clear framework for councils and mayors to follow that will set out recommended terms for local benefit, including an indicative contribution – likely to be financial or in terms of facilities – scaled to a site’s size.

Opposition to datacentre construction is being fuelled by widening public concern about the safety of AI systems, after a summer in which some of the largest companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google appeared to lose control of some of their most cutting-edge AIs. Some protesters have begun resorting to direct action and the membership of anti-AI campaign groups has been growing rapidly.

The datacentre companies are determined to head off that opposition. The chair of the SAIL taskforce, Steve Rigby, said: “By establishing a clear prosperity compact between government, industry and local communities, we can build the infrastructure we need, equip our workforce with future-ready skills, and ensure Britain’s digital destiny. This taskforce’s goal isn’t another strategy document, but high-impact actions that materially accelerate the UK’s transition to an AI-enabled economy.”
It has not calculated the cost to central government finances if councils that grant permission to datacentres are allowed to keep all of their business rates.

Responding to the proposals, Joseph Miller, the director of PauseAI UK, which campaigns for a global pause to datacentre buildout, said: “People are going to feel it is undignified to be bought off by huge tech companies who do not share their interests.”

He said tech companies were “absolutely right to be worried” about US-style public opposition to datacentres growing in the UK. Kat Jones, the director of Action to Protect Rural Scotland, which campaigns against datacentres, said tech companies had already “missed the boat on containing community opposition to hyperscale AI datacentres”.

“In Scotland, we have 15 community campaigns already working incredibly hard opposing these environmentally destructive developments locally, and a growing national campaign,” she said. “Even the titanic lobbying efforts of US big tech are going to find it a real challenge to change the winds of public opinion, which have already shifted solidly against hyperscale AI datacentres.”

Donald Campbell, the director of advocacy at the tech equity campaign Foxglove, said: “Big tech firms have spent years trying to force vast, highly polluting datacentres through the planning system under a blanket of secrecy and misleading information. Now, with the public waking up to the fact that these facilities plunder resources and wreck the climate, the US tech giants have decided that there’s a problem.”

He warned that incentivising councils to back datacentres by allowing them to keep more of their business rate revenue would mean “these wealthy tech giants would not pay a penny more” while boosts to council funding would “come from the pocket of central government services like the NHS”.

A government spokesperson said datacentres “should create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built, as well as prioritising clean power, using water responsibly”.

“For most proposed datacentre developments, community benefits are considered through the relevant local planning processes,” they said. “We have already announced measures which will enable local authorities hosting datacentres in AI growth zones in England to keep all the additional business rates they generate.”

items.title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
paragraphs: For millions of Indians, the road to the ultimate career aspiration had a familiar script - an engineering degree to get a tech services job, then a posting in the US, repeated visa renewals and then the green card that gave them permanent residency in the country.

Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway.

New and pending applications under the Permanent Labor Certification Program, or PERM, have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas - a temporary visa for specialists - which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship.

The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say.
Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300bn (£226bn) technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally.
"Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds.

Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers.

A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.
BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered.
Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them.
But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business.

A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level.

"A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said.
Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders.

Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets.
While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".

While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation.

Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs.
Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all.
Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible.
While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".
Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs.
The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher.

But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process.
Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises.
Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."
While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest.

Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).

Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category.

Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.

Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies.

"This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how.

Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work.

"Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says.

Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.

items.title: Four locations in the running to be UK City of Culture 2029
paragraphs: Blackpool is one of four shortlisted locations to be the next UK City of Culture
Blackpool, Milton Keynes, Sheffield and Wrexham have been shortlisted to become the UK's City of Culture in 2029.
The winning location will be announced in May and will be the fifth holder of the title - following Derry-Londonderry, Hull, Coventry and Bradford.
A different location is given the City of Culture title every four years. Each shortlisted city will now receive at least £125,000 from the government to do further work on their bid.
The eventual winner will receive £10m to deliver a year of cultural events and activities drawing on its "local strengths and stories".
Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the shortlisted cities "have shown the pride that exists in their places with the incredible culture on their doorsteps".
Three of the contenders are in England and one in Wales. They were chosen from a longlist of nine, which also included Inverness, Ipswich, Middlesbrough, Portsmouth and Swindon.

What is it known for? Its landmark Blackpool Tower, Pleasure Beach and Illuminations. It also hosts a major dance festival and an annual visit from Strictly Come Dancing. The Showtown museum celebrates Blackpool's history as a showbiz and comedy hotspot.

What have they said? Lynn Williams, leader of Blackpool Council, said: "Blackpool has been entertaining people for generations, and now we have the chance to show the country exactly what our town is made of."
She added: "Blackpool has never been a town that stands still. It is proud, working-class culture that has always been about bringing people together, having fun and making something happen."

What is it known for? Constructed in the 1960s and 70s, Milton Keynes is known for its US-style grid road system and numerous roundabouts. It is home to historic World War II codebreaking centre Bletchley Park, now a museum, and the National Bowl, an amphitheatre that has hosted concerts by Oasis, Queen and David Bowie.
What have they said? Milton Keynes' bid described it as "a city built on imagination – a place where innovation, diversity and creativity thrive side by side".

Councillor Jane Carr, leader of Milton Keynes City Council, said: "We're now on the cusp of the 60th anniversary of our founding and have so much to look forward to during this landmark year and beyond."

What is it known for? The traditional centre of steel and cutlery manufacturing, Sheffield has since become known for musical exports like the Arctic Monkeys and Pulp, for its annual documentary film festival, and for the Crucible - one of the leading theatres outside London.
What have they said? The city's bid put its spotlight on Sheffield's "world-renowned creative heritage, as well as our ambitious future plans".

Celebrating its place on the shortlist, councillor Fran Belbin, leader of the city council, said: "Sheffield is a city built on creativity, innovation and community spirit... Culture is part of who we are."

What is it known for? North Wales's largest city was a powerhouse of the industrial revolution, and most recently hit the headlines when its historic football club Wrexham AFC was bought by Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob McElhenney.
What have they said? The bid said: "Our ambition is simple but bold: to make Wrexham the world's most playful place."

Joanna Knight OBE, chair of the Wrexham bid, styled as Wrecsam2029, explained: "There's a real sense that something very special is happening here. Just imagine what becoming the first Welsh UK City of Culture could mean... the opportunities are enormous."
Do you live in one of the shortlisted cities? What do you love about your city?

items.title: US adds wrongful detention warning to China travel advisory
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

The U.S. State Department has added a wrongful detention warning to its travel advisory for mainland China, cautioning that Americans face a serious risk of being detained without a fair legal process.
The advisory, updated October 19, keeps China at Level 2 — “Exercise Increased Caution” but adds a “D” risk indicator for wrongful detention.
The advisory warns that Chinese authorities may enforce local laws arbitrarily and impose exit bans without a fair and transparent legal process.
In an emailed statement to VOA, the State Department said it had determined that “Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention in China.”

“The Trump Administration has no higher priority than the safety and security of Americans,” a State Department spokesperson told VOA, adding that the administration was committed to securing the release of Americans wrongfully detained overseas.

The department identifies several groups that may face heightened risks, including Americans of Chinese descent, people involved in business disputes, and those with current or past ties to U.S. law enforcement, the military, intelligence agencies or the federal government.
The House Select Committee on China called the new “D” indicator “a serious warning to all Americans” in a social media post Tuesday.
The State Department has formally designated two U.S. citizens detained in China as wrongfully detained: Chinese American seismologist Chen Youlin and Myanmar-born American scholar Min Zin.
Chen had worked with Chinese researchers on a U.S. government-funded public research project examining seismic signals from underground nuclear tests in North Korea.

Chinese authorities arrested Chen on November 5, 2024, as he prepared to return to the United States after visiting family in China. On May 1, 2025, China accused him of espionage. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention in March 2026.

Min Zin, who studies Myanmar politics and China-Myanmar relations, was detained by Chinese authorities after traveling to China’s southern Yunnan province for a conference in June this year. Beijing accused him of suspected espionage that endangered China's national security. The State Department designated his case as wrongful detention on August 20.
The designations make securing the release of both men a U.S. government priority.
President Donald Trump said he raised the cases of detained Americans and Chinese political prisoners with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their White House meeting at the end of September.
The State Department also confirmed to VOA that Washington had directly raised Chen's and Min Zin's cases with Beijing.
Chen's wife, Rong Yufang, welcomed the updated travel advisory in a written statement sent to VOA through Global Reach, a nonprofit organization working to secure her husband's release.

“I am grateful to Secretary Rubio for taking this action,” she said. “He has tried for months to quietly resolve my husband’s wrongful detention in China, and President Trump has even asked President Xi twice about Youlin.”

Aung Maw Zin, Min Zin’s brother, told VOA on Wednesday that “we are glad to see this small but important step that could help ensure that no other American family has to endure the nightmare our family has been living through since June.”

The United States previously placed China at Level 3, with a “D” indicator for wrongful detention. The advisory was downgraded to Level 2 and the indicator removed on November 27, 2024, after three Americans detained in China for years were released in a prisoner exchange between Washington and Beijing.
Upcoming summits could bring renewed pressure
Eric Lebson, chief strategy officer at Global Reach, told VOA that the espionage allegations against Chen were fabricated.
Lebson said Trump could press for a resolution when he meets Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen and the G20 meeting at Mar-a-Lago over the next two months.
“President Xi can expect President Trump to continue raising the need to resolve this case while the State Department increases the costs associated with holding two U.S. citizens,” Lebson said.

Beijing has rejected allegations of wrongful detention, maintaining that its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law.The Chinese Embassy in Washington has yet not responded to VOA's request for comment.

items.title: US says wartime command transfer to South Korea remains conditions based
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

The United States has reiterated that wartime operational control, or OPCON, of allied forces on the Korean Peninsula will transition to South Korea only after mutually agreed conditions are met, despite renewed calls from Seoul to accelerate the process.

“The transition of wartime operational control (OPCON) remains a conditions-based process mutually agreed upon by the United States and the Republic of Korea,” a U.S. Department of Defense official told VOA on Monday, speaking on background.

“Both nations remain committed to ensuring that the necessary conditions are met before any transition occurs,” the official said. “We will not prejudge decisions or outcomes of this bilateral process.”
Wartime OPCON refers to the authority to direct military operations during a conflict.

Under the current U.S.-South Korea combined defense structure, a U.S. general serves as commander of the Combined Forces Command, which would oversee allied military operations in wartime. CFC was established in 1978 with a goal to "deter, or defeat if necessary, outside aggression against" South Korea. It unified U.S. and South Korean forces under a single war-fighting command.

Although South Korea regained peacetime OPCON in 1994, plans to transfer wartime OPCON were repeatedly postponed before the allies adopted a conditions-based approach in 2014, leaving the timing of the transition undecided.
The comments come as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung pushes for a faster transition of wartime command authority.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Lee said South Korea should “swiftly” regain wartime OPCON, arguing that the country possesses sufficient military capabilities to assume greater responsibility for its own defense. According to South Korean media reports, Lee suggested that “regaining” or “restoring” wartime OPCON would be more appropriate terms than “transferring” it.

The issue gained renewed attention last week after Gen. Xavier Brunson, commander of U.S. Forces Korea, said the conditions surrounding the transition had evolved since the allies established their original framework.

“Because the conditions have changed, because we’ve changed our plan, we have new standards which we have to uphold,” Brunson said at a policy forum in Washington, citing an evolving security environment that includes North Korea’s continued weapons development and recent missile activities.
The Pentagon did not say whether the formal criteria for the transition had been revised.

The two allies have agreed to a conditions-based process that includes assessments of South Korea’s military capabilities and its ability to lead combined operations. While the Lee administration has expressed interest in completing the transition before the end of its term in 2030, Washington and Seoul have not publicly announced a target date.
Patrick Cronin, chair for Asia-Pacific security at the Hudson Institute, told VOA earlier this year that the OPCON transition carries both political and military significance.

Politically, the transition symbolizes “regaining full sovereignty” for many South Koreans, Cronin said. Militarily, however, he argued that the focus should remain on how the change would affect deterrence and the alliance’s ability to respond effectively to regional threats.
Sungwon Baik from VOA's Korean service contributed to this report.
